focus: Exodus 27 moves outward from the tent to the bronze altar of burnt offering and the courtyard that surrounds the tabernacle, with its single gate. The chapter ends by turning back inside the tent to command pure olive oil for the lamp, which Aaron and his sons are to keep burning before the LORD.

sections.title: The Bronze Altar
sections.summary: Israel is to make a square altar of acacia wood overlaid with bronze, with horns of one piece with it, a bronze grate, and bronze utensils. It is to be hollow, carried by poles, and made “as it was shown you on the mountain” (Exodus 27:8).

sections.title: The Courtyard and Its Gate
sections.summary: A courtyard one hundred cubits long and fifty wide is enclosed with hangings of fine linen on pillars set in bronze sockets with silver hooks and bands. On the east side a woven screen twenty cubits long forms the gate of the court, and all the pegs and utensils for the service are bronze.

sections.title: Pure Oil for the Lamp That Burns Before the LORD
sections.summary: Israel is to bring pure oil of pressed olives “to cause the lamp to burn continually” (Exodus 27:20). Aaron and his sons are to tend it from evening until morning before the LORD, outside the veil, as a statute forever.

1.brief: Israel is to make an altar of acacia wood, five cubits square and three cubits high. The altar of burnt offering will stand in the courtyard.
1.explain:
“You shall make an altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits wide—the altar shall be square—”

The instructions move outside the tent to the courtyard. “An altar” of acacia wood is made, about seven and a half feet square.

“and its height shall be three cubits.”

It stood about four and a half feet high. This was the altar of burnt offering, where the daily sacrifices were made (29:38–42). It stood just inside the courtyard gate, in front of the tent (40:29).

2.brief: Horns are made on its four corners, of one piece with it, and it is overlaid with bronze. The horned altar is prepared for sacrifice.
2.explain:
“You shall make its horns on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it.”

“Horns” project from the four corners, made “of one piece” with the altar. Blood from sin offerings was put on the horns (29:12; Leviticus 4:7).

“And you shall overlay it with bronze.”

The altar is covered with “bronze,” which could withstand the fire. The horned altar is prepared for sacrifice.
2.notes: People seeking mercy sometimes took hold of the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:50–51; 2:28). The law did not protect a deliberate murderer there (21:14).

3.brief: Its pans, shovels, basins, forks, and firepans are all made of bronze. The tools for the altar’s daily service are provided.
3.explain:
“Also you shall make its pans to receive its ashes, and its shovels and its basins and its forks and its firepans;”

The altar’s tools are listed: “pans” for ashes, “shovels,” “basins” for blood, “forks” for handling the meat, and “firepans” for carrying coals.

“you shall make all its utensils of bronze.”

All are “of bronze.” The tools for the altar’s daily service are provided.

4.brief: A grate of bronze network is made for the altar, with four bronze rings at its four corners. The netlike grate is part of the altar’s structure.
4.explain:
“You shall make a grate for it, a network of bronze;”

A “grate,” a mesh of bronze, is made for the altar.

“and on the network you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners.”

The grate has “four bronze rings” at its corners. The netlike grate is part of the altar’s structure.

5.brief: The grate is placed under the altar’s rim, halfway up. The grate is set within the altar.
5.explain:
“You shall put it under the rim of the altar beneath, that the network may be midway up the altar.”

The grate sits “midway up the altar,” under a ledge. Its exact function is uncertain. It may have supported the fire or formed a decorative band on the outside. The grate is set within the altar.

6.brief: Poles of acacia wood overlaid with bronze are made for the altar. The altar, like the other furnishings, is made to travel.
6.explain:
“And you shall make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with bronze.”

The altar also has carrying “poles,” overlaid with “bronze” to match it. The altar, like the other furnishings, is made to travel.

7.brief: The poles are put in the rings on the two sides to carry it. The altar moves with Israel.
7.explain:
“The poles shall be put in the rings, and the poles shall be on the two sides of the altar to bear it.”

The poles go through the rings to carry the altar. The altar moves with Israel.

8.brief: The altar is to be hollow, made with boards, “as it was shown you on the mountain.” Even the altar’s construction follows God’s pattern.
8.explain:
“You shall make it hollow with boards;”

The altar is “hollow,” a box frame without top or bottom. When set up, it may have been filled with earth or stones (compare 20:24–25).

“as it was shown you on the mountain, so shall they make it.”

The altar too follows God’s pattern. Even the altar’s construction follows God’s design. The bronze altar points to Christ’s once-for-all offering. Hebrews says believers “have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all,” and that “by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:10, 14). The altar stood between the courtyard gate and the tent, so no one approached the dwelling without passing the place of sacrifice.

9.brief: The court of the tabernacle is to have hangings of fine woven linen one hundred cubits long on the south side. A courtyard will surround God’s dwelling.
9.explain:
“You shall also make the court of the tabernacle.”

A “court” or courtyard surrounds the tabernacle.

“For the south side there shall be hangings for the court made of fine woven linen, one hundred cubits long for one side.”

Its walls are “hangings” of “fine woven linen.” The south side is “one hundred cubits” long, about 150 feet. A courtyard will surround God’s dwelling.

10.brief: Its twenty pillars and sockets are bronze, with silver hooks and bands. The court’s structure combines bronze and silver.
10.explain:
“And its twenty pillars and their twenty sockets shall be bronze.”

“Twenty pillars” on “bronze” sockets support the south side.

“The hooks of the pillars and their bands shall be silver.”

Their “hooks” and “bands” are silver. The court’s structure combines bronze and silver.

11.brief: The north side also has one hundred cubits of hangings with twenty pillars and bronze sockets, with silver hooks and bands. The long sides match.
11.explain:
“Likewise along the length of the north side there shall be hangings one hundred cubits long,”

The north side matches the south.

“with its twenty pillars and their twenty sockets of bronze, and the hooks of the pillars and their bands of silver.”

It has the same pillars, sockets, hooks, and bands. The long sides match.

12.brief: The west side has fifty cubits of hangings with ten pillars and ten sockets. The rear of the court is closed.
12.explain:
“And along the width of the court on the west side shall be hangings of fifty cubits, with their ten pillars and their ten sockets.”

The west side, the back, is “fifty cubits,” about 75 feet, with “ten pillars.” The rear of the court is closed.

13.brief: The east side of the court is fifty cubits wide. The front of the court faces east.
13.explain:
“The width of the court on the east side shall be fifty cubits.”

The east side, the front, is also fifty cubits wide. The front of the court faces east.

14.brief: Hangings of fifteen cubits with three pillars and sockets are on one side of the gate. The east side is built around an opening.
14.explain:
“The hangings on one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and their three sockets.”

On one side of the gate are fifteen cubits of hangings. The east side is built around an opening.

15.brief: Matching hangings of fifteen cubits with three pillars and sockets are on the other side. The entrance is framed symmetrically.
15.explain:
“And on the other side shall be hangings of fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and their three sockets.”

Matching hangings stand on the other side. The entrance is framed symmetrically.

16.brief: The gate of the court has a screen twenty cubits long of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with four pillars and sockets. God provides one wide and beautiful entrance into the court.
16.explain:
“For the gate of the court there shall be a screen twenty cubits long,”

“The gate of the court” is “twenty cubits,” about 30 feet wide. There is only one entrance into the courtyard.

“woven of blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and fine woven linen, made by a weaver. It shall have four pillars and four sockets.”

The gate’s screen is colorful, unlike the plain white linen walls. It is easy to find. God provides one wide and beautiful entrance into the court. The single entrance pictures Jesus, the way to the Father. Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6), and “I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

17.brief: All the court’s pillars have silver bands, silver hooks, and bronze sockets. The court is finished consistently all around.
17.explain:
“All the pillars around the court shall have bands of silver; their hooks shall be of silver and their sockets of bronze.”

Every pillar around the court has silver bands and hooks and bronze sockets. The court is finished consistently all around.

18.brief: The court is one hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and five high, of fine linen with bronze sockets. The verse gives the court’s overall size.
18.explain:
“The length of the court shall be one hundred cubits, the width fifty throughout, and the height five cubits,”

The court is about 150 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 7 and a half feet high. The walls were above eye level.

“made of fine woven linen, and its sockets of bronze.”

The verse gives the court’s overall size and materials.

19.brief: All the utensils for the tabernacle’s service and all its pegs and the court’s pegs are bronze. Even the smallest parts are provided.
19.explain:
“All the utensils of the tabernacle for all its service, all its pegs, and all the pegs of the court, shall be of bronze.”

Even the “pegs” that anchored the tent cords were bronze. Even the smallest parts are provided for.

20.brief: Israel is to bring pure oil of pressed olives for the light, “to cause the lamp to burn continually.” The people supply the oil that keeps the light burning before God.
20.explain:
“And you shall command the children of Israel that they bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light,”

The people must supply “pure oil of pressed olives.” The finest oil came from olives crushed by hand. It was clear and burned with little smoke.

“to cause the lamp to burn continually.”

The oil keeps “the lamp” burning “continually,” that is, every night without fail (27:21). The people supply the oil that keeps the light burning before God. The oil pictures dependence on the Holy Spirit. In Zechariah 4:2–6 a lampstand fed by olive oil is explained with the words, “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,” says the LORD of hosts. The light in the sanctuary also points to Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12).

21.brief: In the tabernacle of meeting, outside the veil, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamp from evening until morning before the LORD as a perpetual statute. The priests keep the light burning through the night in God’s presence.
21.explain:
“In the tabernacle of meeting, outside the veil which is before the Testimony,”

The lampstand stands in “the tabernacle of meeting,” in the holy place “outside the veil.” The name “tabernacle of meeting” describes the tent as the place where God meets with His people.

“Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening until morning before the LORD.”

The priests keep the lamps burning through the whole night in God’s presence.

“It shall be a statute forever to their generations on behalf of the children of Israel.”

This is “a statute forever,” done “on behalf of the children of Israel.” The priests keep the light burning through the night in God’s presence for the whole people.
21.notes: 1 Samuel 3:3 notes that the LORD called the boy Samuel “before the lamp of God went out.”
